case_study_insert.main_stem: Riverbend Veterinary Hospital (RVH) is a public limited company in the veterinary care sector, employing a workforce of 156. Founded in 1998 by Dr Marcus Ellison, RVH is listed on the regional stock exchange and operates a specialist referral hospital using a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. It plans to invest $2,400,000 in a 24-hour emergency and diagnostic service line, financed by a $1,500,000 share issue and $900,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $720,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $22.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. RVH faces routine-appointment waiting lists averaging 18 days, difficult recruitment of qualified veterinary staff, and nurse turnover of 29%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The hospital delivered 20,000 procedure units last quarter at a clinical rework rate of 1.1%, down from 2.4% a year ago. Client complaints fell from 44 to 27 per month. A survey of 900 pet owners found 66% would use a 24-hour emergency service and 39% would pay a monthly health-plan subscription of $24; 52% chose RVH because of its specialist teams. Average waiting time for routine consultations is 18 days, and 28 of 156 staff have not completed training on the new diagnostic imaging suite. Off-the-job training at the veterinary college costs $1,150 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Riverbend Veterinary Hospital for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.45 to $13.26 per hour from April 2026, raising veterinary wage bills. (3) Pet-food and pharmaceutical input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, animal-care inflation is running at 7.9%, and consumer spending on pet insurance grew 5.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: RVH plans to finance part of its 24-hour emergency and diagnostic service line with a share issue. Explain two advantages for RVH of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs RVH nothing in dividends or issue expenses, protecting cash flow for a business already carrying fixed costs of $720,000 a year and a new service line expected to serve heavy demand. Every dollar of spare profit kept inside the company can absorb the 11.2% rise in pet-food and pharmaceutical costs and the upcoming 6.5% minimum wage rise, helping keep the $22.00 average price sustainable while the emergency line beds in.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids diluting existing shareholders' ownership and control, which matters to founder Dr Marcus Ellison and to a regional-exchange investor base watching RVH's reported revenue and operating profit, both shown growing in Appendix 2. It keeps funding internally available without market flotation risk or signalling worries, so the $900,000 stays committed to the service line even if pet-insurance growth of 5.2% plateaus or the 66% of owners willing to use a 24-hour emergency service take longer to convert into bookings, and no new shareholders can demand higher dividends instead of reinvesting in the imaging suite and recruitment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Riverbend Veterinary Hospital, its emergency service line and its cost base.

questions.question_text: RVH is promoting the launch of its 24-hour emergency and diagnostic service line. Consider a national press campaign, local radio sponsorship, or online search and social media advertising. Which should RVH choose to promote the new emergency service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National press campaign: A national press campaign would build strong credibility for RVH's brand and reach pet owners across the country, reinforcing the specialist referral positioning that 52% of surveyed owners value. However, circulation is expensive, much of the readership lies far outside RVH's catchment, and print is poor at reaching owners at the moment of an emergency, so wastage would be large for an 80,000-unit business funding a $2,400,000 expansion partly with a $1,500,000 share issue.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is cheaper than print or national TV and reaches pet owners commuting and listening in RVH's region, keeping the 24-hour line front of mind when accidents happen. However, reach is capped at the region, and radio cannot target urgent-care seekers precisely, so it cannot alone convert the 66% of 900 surveyed owners who said they would use a 24-hour service into registered, pre-authorised customers.

Online search and social media advertising: Search and social ads let RVH appear exactly when owners search emergency vet services, and social targeting can reach the 66% likely to use the 24-hour service and the 39% willing to pay a $24 monthly health-plan subscription. Results are measurable per click and booking, budgets are controllable, and the approach suits the diagnostic-suite story; however, it depends on rapid response and good ad quality rather than deep editorial credibility.

Recommendation: RVH should choose online search and social media advertising. It meets pet owners at the precise moment of need, is measurable and budget-flexible against a $2,400,000 investment, and converts the surveyed demand directly into bookings. National press is rejected as too expensive and too untargeted for emergency care, and local radio is rejected as too broad and too weak at intercepting the emergency moment — it can reinforce awareness, not lead the campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RVH with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of RVH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the press campaign and radio sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: RVH uses laissez-faire leadership for its specialist clinical teams. Explain two benefits for RVH of this leadership approach for motivation among its senior veterinary staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives senior veterinary specialists real autonomy to design treatment protocols, allocate diagnostic resources and run their own theatre lists without constant supervision. This trust meets esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow), makes senior clinicians feel valued as experts, and strengthens motivation at a time when retaining talent is hard — 29% nurse turnover suggests frontline morale needs protecting through visible trust in senior staff and competitive employer branding; unmediated case reviews keep senior clinicians accountable to outcomes they value.

Point 2: Autonomy lets specialist teams respond fast to complex referrals, improving the clinical outcomes that 52% of surveyed owners associate with RVH's specialist reputation. Empowered senior clinicians develop new service lines such as the 24-hour emergency unit, innovate with the diagnostic imaging suite, and mentor junior staff, reducing dependence on external recruitment in a tight labour market while RVH targets the demand shown by the 66% of owners wanting 24-hour cover; that autonomy also protects quality while the 18-day waiting list stabilises and complaints fall.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RVH's specialist model, turnover and emergency service line.

questions.question_text: RVH must train the 28 staff who have not completed training on the new diagnostic imaging suite. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the veterinary college. Which should RVH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training beside the imaging technicians already using the suite is directly relevant to RVH's exact machines, protocols and emergency workflows, costs no fees and keeps the 28 staff productive for patients with 18-day routine waiting lists and growing emergency demand. However, it depends on senior radiographer availability, can pass on workarounds instead of best practice, and gives no formal certificate that supports the rework rate already falling from 2.4% to 1.1%.

Off-the-job training at the veterinary college: College courses at $1,150 per employee give structured, accredited imaging skills for all 28 staff at $32,200 in total — modest against a $2,400,000 investment and $900,000 retained profit. However, staff are absent from clinics for days, routine and emergency capacity is strained, content is generic rather than tied to RVH's suite, and back-fill or overtime would be needed given recruitment is already difficult and 29% nurse turnover.

Decision: RVH should choose on-the-job training for the 28 staff, anchored by a short off-the-job college certificate only for the four imaging leads. On-the-job delivery is machine-specific, keeps the emergency line usable and avoids deeper list delays; full off-the-job training is rejected because $32,200 plus 28 absent staff would worsen the 18-day waiting list and slow the launch of the $2,400,000 emergency and diagnostic service line. College certification for the leads secures standards and satisfies insurers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to RVH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of RVH.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of RVH with a well-justified decision covering cost, waiting lists, equipment relevance and the emergency service line.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RVH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $720,000 ÷ ($22.00 − $12.00) = $720,000 ÷ $10.00 = 72,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 72,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $22.00 − $12.00 = $10.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $10.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RVH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 72,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 80,000 units to see that a margin of safety of only 8,000 units leaves thin headroom, flagging the risk of the new emergency line underperforming before it ramps up.
2. Use contribution per unit of $10.00 to model the $24 monthly health-plan subscription wanted by 39% of owners, testing whether subscription revenue covers the emergency line's fixed-cost share before launch.
3. Stress-test the $2,400,000 financing mix of share issue and retained profit by checking the 8,000-unit margin of safety against repayment and dividend obligations and against the 11.2% pharmaceutical cost rise.
4. Benchmark unit cost ($720,000 ÷ 80,000 units + $12.00 = $21.00 a unit) across quarters to attack the 1.1% rework rate, challenge pharmaceutical purchasing amid the 11.2% input inflation and track productivity against the 20,000 procedure units delivered last quarter.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 72,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $10.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 8,000 units against 80,000-unit output; subscription pricing modelling against the $720,000 fixed costs; stress-testing the $2,400,000 expansion financing; unit-cost benchmarking at $21.00 to drive the 11.2% input-cost response and rework reduction.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RVH's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has RVH's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.5%
ROCE 2025 = 16.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $600,000 on revenue $1,500,000 (cost of sales $900,000); 2025 gross profit $792,000 on revenue $1,760,000 (cost of sales $968,000). 2024 operating profit $225,000; 2025 operating profit $352,000. 2024 capital employed $1,800,000; 2025 capital employed $2,200,000. Interest payable rose from $28,000 to $36,000.

Evaluation: Underlying performance improved clearly. Revenue grew $260,000 (17.3%) while cost of sales as a share of revenue fell from 60.0% to 55.0%, lifting gross profit from $600,000 to $792,000 (32.0%) — helped by rework falling from 2.4% to 1.1% and complaints from 44 to 27 per month. Operating profit grew from $225,000 to $352,000 (56.4%), comfortably ahead of revenue growth, so overheads were absorbed well. Capital employed rose $400,000, consistent with the emergency service line investment, yet the return on that capital still strengthened from 12.5% to 16.0%. However, pharmaceutical-cost inflation of 11.2% threatens the cost line in 2026, interest charges are climbing, and the 18-day waiting list plus 29% nurse turnover could dent future activity if unaddressed.

Conclusion: Yes, RVH's financial performance has improved. Revenue, gross profit and operating profit all rose strongly and the return on capital employed climbed from 12.5% to 16.0%, driven by genuine cost control rather than price alone. The judgement is not risk-free — input costs, interest and staffing risks persist — so RVH should lock in pharmaceutical purchasing, fix rates where possible and accelerate the emergency launch to convert waiting-list demand into completed procedures.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, interest and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether RVH's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RVH of launching a monthly pet health-plan subscription at $24.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A subscription converts occasional visits into predictable recurring revenue, smoothing the peaks that stretch the hospital's 80,000-unit capacity and its 18-day routine waiting list. With 39% of the 900 surveyed owners willing to pay $24 a month, RVH could bank meaningful guaranteed income to service the $2,400,000 emergency investment and fund nurse retention in the face of 29% turnover, while deepening loyalty with the 66% likely to use the 24-hour service; a subscription base also gives RVH steadier footfall around which to plan staff rotas.

Disadvantage: Subscriptions shift risk onto RVH if promised checks and vaccinations cost more than the fees collected, compressing the $10.00 contribution per unit if take-up of complex cases exceeds pricing. Administering monthly billing, reminders and plan audits adds overhead before the service line matures, and any perceived decline in service quality could trigger cancellations, complaints (already 27 a month) and reputational damage among the 52% who chose RVH for its specialist teams; clear plan terms and annual reviews would be needed to control that risk.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RVH's survey data, costs and emergency investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in pet-food and pharmaceutical costs will affect RVH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): A 0.75 percentage point rise increases borrowing costs for any variable-rate facilities, though the insert shows no such borrowing attached to RVH's expansion — it is financed by a $1,500,000 share issue and $900,000 retained profit. Each $1,000,000 of variable-rate borrowing would cost about $7,500 more per year (0.75% × $1,000,000, computable), so if any element of its banking were variable-rate the charge would rise above the $36,000 interest payable shown in 2025. The rise could also dampen pet owners' willingness to fund care, but the effect is the smallest of the three changes given the equity-heavy financing structure shown in the extract.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.26 per hour): The rise is $0.81 an hour ($13.26 − $12.45, both insert figures) on every minimum-wage hour worked. Senior vets and nurses earn well above the minimum wage, so the increase falls only on entry-level duties; the insert gives no wage-bill total or hours worked, so the exact annual cost cannot be quantified from the figures provided. What is certain is that it is permanent, applies hourly to the lowest-paid roles, and adds pressure at a time when recruitment of qualified staff is already difficult and nurse turnover stands at 29%.

Input cost inflation (11.2% pet food and pharmaceuticals): Pet food and pharmaceuticals — a major element of the $12.00 variable cost per unit — have risen 11.2% year-on-year; across 80,000 units the variable-cost spend pools to $960,000 ($12.00 × 80,000, computable from the insert). The extract does not split pharmaceuticals from other variable costs, so the precise annual impact cannot be computed, but an 11.2% rise raises the cost of every procedure on both the emergency line and routine clinics, and threatens the fall in cost of sales as a share of revenue from 60.0% to 55.0% and the gross profit growth from $600,000 to $792,000 that RVH has worked to achieve.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in pet-food and pharmaceutical costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 80,000 units at about $67,000 a year of lost contribution — exceeding the roughly $43,000 wage impact and dwarfing the modest interest-rate effect on RVH's share-funded expansion. The wage rise is the second most serious risk; the interest rise is the smallest, but both still demand tighter purchasing, fee reviews and careful financial control.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to RVH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RVH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of RVH with a well-justified judgement that pet-food and pharmaceutical inflation has the greatest impact, and why the wage rise and the interest rise are smaller.
